title: Gabriel Santos - ASCII Art Techniques & Animation
speaker: Gabriel Santos
summary: Gabriel Santos, presenting entirely in ASCII, walks through six years of techniques for ASCII line art and animation developed for his game. He covers scene layering, a simple ASCII particle emitter, styles of text art (block, line, box drawing), font aspect ratios and multi-size fonts, glyph choice and avoiding alphanumerics, line angles and anti-aliasing, negative space, dithering, accidental shadows, and subtractive animation. He includes a live drawing demo to argue that ASCII art is fast to iterate on once glyph combinations are memorized.

insights.claim: ASCII animated scenes can be built from separate layers: a static background plus independently animated characters and small details.
insights.detail: Santos decomposes his cultist scene into a background layer, an animation for each cultist, the victim, and small details like a chain and a one-glyph candle flame that animate separately.
insights.quote: I want to show how this scene is decomposed. So there's a background layer, and here's the animation for the cultist.

insights.claim: A deliberately simple ASCII particle emitter, with only velocity and glyphs and emission points stored as metadata in the art, is enough for effective effects.
insights.detail: Santos's emitter has no particle interaction like smoke systems do; it just moves ASCII symbols with velocity and can fit two particles in one cell. He argues this is how projects should be: simple and getting the job done.
insights.quote: It just has velocity and it shows the ASCII symbols. It's able to fit two particles within the same cell

insights.claim: Modern ASCII art should use Unicode symbols where they help, but only ones that retain the established visual style.
insights.detail: Santos's art is not strictly traditional ASCII; he argues modern computers make Unicode available and you should leverage it while keeping style consistent.
insights.quote: in modern computers, you should leverage that. But I wanted to stick to the style, so I used Unicode symbols that retained the style.

insights.claim: Text art has distinct styles: block art for filled shapes, line art for organic objects, and box drawing for geometric, mechanical things and UI.
insights.detail: Block art is what automatic video-to-ASCII conversion produces. Santos focuses on line art for organic forms; box drawing suits mechanical subjects, as in Cogmind, a game about robots, and UI elements like buttons and scroll windows.
insights.quote: you get more organic characters and organic objects when you do line art, and you get more geometric, more mechanical things when you do box drawing

insights.claim: A 1:1 font aspect ratio suits top-down ASCII games, while side or isometric views work better near 1:2.
insights.detail: After much experimentation Santos settled on 16:29 for his side-view game. His font is a spinoff of Courier.
insights.quote: 1:1 is really good for top-down games, but if you're going for an isometric perspective or side perspective, like I'm doing, 1:2 is better

insights.claim: Shipping many pixel-exact sizes of the same font lets an ASCII game stay pixel perfect at any window resolution by choosing the font dynamically.
insights.detail: Santos had over 20 sizes made, the smallest 3x5 pixels, and says the game still reads at that size.
insights.quote: I wanted the game to be pixel perfect at any resolution. You're able to scale the window size and it picks the font dynamically.

insights.claim: Letters and digits placed inside ASCII art draw the eye first and get read as text, so they are usually an unwanted distraction.
insights.detail: Santos says alphanumerics affect a different part of the brain; use them only purposefully. Symbols like the inverted exclamation mark (for anti-aliasing) and the centre dot (for balance and negative space) fit the line-art style better.
insights.quote: you need to be aware that that's where the eye's gonna be drawn to first

insights.claim: Drawing the same line angle with different glyph combinations can encode materials such as metal, wood or rock, if used consistently.
insights.detail: Santos shows two glyph treatments of the same angle and says the reader will internalize a consistent mapping, letting you paint a bigger picture with that language.
insights.quote: if you're consistent in that, the reader will internalize that, and you can then paint a bigger picture, using that language

insights.claim: ASCII line art struggles with near-vertical lines because glyphs are horizontally aligned, which calls for anti-aliasing tricks using marks like exclamation points and quotes.
insights.detail: Horizontal-ish lines have many glyph gradations within a cell, but angles between 60 and 90 degrees do not; the naive result looks jagged, acceptable for rock or spiderweb but not smooth surfaces. Santos shows several anti-aliased versions of the same angle and curve.
insights.quote: with the vertical lines, you don't, because all the glyphs are horizontally aligned. So you can't really do lines between 90 degrees and 60 degrees.

insights.claim: ASCII art is faster to iterate than other art media once common glyph combinations are memorized, so you can quickly try several variants and choose.
insights.detail: In a live demo Santos draws a jack-o-lantern and swaps three versions of the mouth in moments, arguing iteration and exploration are really important.
insights.quote: iteration and exploration is really important, and with this example here, you can see how efficient it actually can be

insights.claim: Inserting empty cells where overlapping ASCII shapes touch separates objects, adds depth and makes scenes read faster; colour shifts can do the same.
insights.detail: Santos shows overlapping circles and a robot guardian's shoulder and belt where gaps make foreground parts read as being on top; connecting them would make the arm unreadable. Shading one object light grey also adds depth.
insights.quote: you can swap some of these glyphs and just add some empty space, and it gives it more depth and reads faster, separates the objects from each other

insights.claim: In ASCII, characters with blank space below them read as shadows when walking over a patterned or textured floor.
insights.detail: Santos discovered this accidentally on a patterned temple floor and now adds shadows to everything. He also uses dithering, borrowed from pixel art, for lighting.
insights.quote: So it works very effectively, if you have a pattern or a texture on the ground.

insights.claim: ASCII animation follows the same process as other animation: references, concepts, a key idle pose, and testing size and composition in context before spending hours animating.
insights.detail: Santos warns that skipping the in-context size test means redoing work or clipping the character's head, which happened to him.
insights.quote: you need to test that within the context, to make sure you have the size correct and the composition correct, before you start animating

insights.claim: Build-up animations can be made subtractively: draw the finished image, remove a piece per frame, then play the frames in reverse.
insights.detail: Santos made a pyramid building brick by brick by drawing it complete and deleting a brick each frame, then reordering frames.
insights.quote: I first drew the pyramid completely, and then, for each frame, I removed a brick. So you do it the other way around.

insights.claim: Small glyph swaps change perceived lighting and vertical centering in ASCII art, such as using a solid box-drawing line instead of hyphens.
insights.detail: In iterating his logo, Santos replaced hyphens (which leave gaps and change the lighting) with a box-drawing line, making it brighter at the top, darker at the bottom and better centred in the font.
insights.quote: if you use the hyphen here, you get these empty spaces in between, and that changes the lighting
